question: When you are taking a nursing history from a patient, what kind of information are you mainly collecting?
explanation: You've got this! History taking is all about listening to what the patient tells you about how they feel. That direct information is called subjective data. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h1)

question: Why is taking a good patient history considered the bedrock of your clinical nursing practice?

options.A: It provides definitive proof of a medical diagnosis
options.B: It replaces the need for any laboratory investigations
options.C: It guides your physical assessment and care planning
options.D: It eliminates all risks of clinical documentation errors

explanation: Spot on! A thorough history points you in the right direction, helping you know where to focus your physical exam and how to plan the best care. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h1)

question: Which body language habit helps your patient feel trusted and relaxed during an interview?
explanation: Well done! Keeping an open posture shows your patient you are warm, friendly, and genuinely ready to listen to their story. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h2)

question: Why is it so important to build quick rapport with a patient right at the start of an interview?

options.A: It prevents the patient from asking any difficult questions
options.B: It shortens the total time needed for the physical exam
options.C: It guarantees the patient will follow all medication orders
options.D: It lowers patient anxiety and encourages honest sharing

explanation: Exactly! When patients feel safe and respected by you, they relax and open up about what is truly bothering them. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h2)

question: What is the main goal of using an open-ended question when talking to a patient?

options.A: To let patients tell their story in their own words
options.B: To test the patient's memory on past surgeries
options.C: To get a quick yes or no answer about a symptom
options.D: To confirm the exact date a medication was started

explanation: You got it! Open-ended questions give patients the freedom to express their concerns naturally without feeling rushed or boxed in. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h3)

question: A patient tells you, 'Nurse, I just don't feel right.' Which response is the best example of a clarifying question?

options.A: Take this thermometer and check your temperature immediately.
options.B: Why did you wait so long before coming to the clinic?
options.C: Do you have a headache, fever, or stomach pain right now?
options.D: Can you tell me more about what 'not feeling right' feels like?

explanation: Brilliant! Asking them to describe a vague feeling helps you get clear, specific details instead of guessing. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h3)

question: In the popular OLDCARTS pain assessment mnemonic, what does the letter 'L' stand for?
explanation: Correct! 'L' stands for location. It helps you pinpoint exactly where on the body the patient is hurting. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h4)

question: When a patient has tummy pain, asking what makes the pain better or worse helps you figure out what?

options.A: The patient's family history of illness
options.C: The exact medical diagnosis of the disease

explanation: Spot on! Finding out what triggers or soothes the pain helps you identify its relieving and aggravating factors. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h4)

question: When you are taking a family health history, which group of relatives should you focus on first?

options.A: Neighbors living in the same community
options.C: First-degree relatives like parents and siblings

explanation: You nailed it! Parents, brothers, and sisters share the closest genetic traits with your patient, so their medical history matters most. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h5)

question: Why is it so crucial to ask a patient about their past medical history?

options.A: It reveals chronic conditions that affect current symptoms
options.B: It tells you what the patient eats for breakfast
options.C: It replaces the need to ask about the present illness
options.D: It proves whether the patient takes their medication daily

explanation: Exactly! Knowing past health issues helps you understand how older illnesses might be mixing with or causing today's trouble. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h5)

question: Why is it important to ask a patient about their job and workplace environment during a social history?

options.A: It helps calculate the exact monthly income of the patient
options.B: It determines how many days off work the patient needs
options.C: Certain jobs expose workers to toxins that cause chronic illness
options.D: It shows whether the patient enjoys their daily job duties

explanation: Well reasoned! Workplace exposures like dust, fumes, or heavy lifting often play a big role in lung or body pains. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h6)

question: If a patient casually mentions they drink a lot of alcohol when you ask about social habits, what should be your first nursing reaction?

options.A: Tell the patient they must stop drinking today
options.B: Acknowledge the disclosure calmly without showing judgment
options.C: Immediately document that the patient has an addiction
options.D: Scold the patient for damaging their liver health

explanation: Spot on! Keeping a cool, non-judgmental attitude makes the patient feel safe enough to keep telling you the truth. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h6)

question: What is the main goal of doing a review of systems during an interview?

options.A: To perform a complete hands-on physical examination
options.B: To diagnose every chronic disease the patient has
options.C: To test the patient's knowledge of anatomy and physiology
options.D: To uncover symptoms the patient may have forgotten or omitted

explanation: You got it! The review of systems acts as a helpful safety net to catch any symptoms the patient forgot to mention. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h7)

question: How should you as a nurse organize your questions when running through a review of systems?

options.A: Let the patient talk freely without any guided direction
options.B: Ask targeted questions system by system from head to toe
options.C: Ask the patient to list every illness they had as a child
options.D: Focus only on the exact organ system of the main complaint

explanation: Brilliant! Going step-by-step from the head down ensures you never accidentally leave out an important body system. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h7)

question: What is the best way to write down a patient's chief complaint in their clinical chart?

options.A: Use the patient's own words inside quotation marks
options.B: Translate their description into complex medical jargon
options.C: Leave the exact wording out and just write your diagnosis
options.D: Summarize what you think they meant in your own words

explanation: Correct! Putting their exact words in quotes keeps their story pure without adding your own guesswork. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h8)

question: Which of these actions is a serious breach of ethical nursing practice when taking a history?

options.A: Asking a family member to step out while taking a sensitive history
options.B: Discussing a patient's medical history in a public hospital hallway
options.C: Asking clarifying questions about the onset of a headache
options.D: Documenting the patient's social habits in their official chart

explanation: Well done! Talking about patient health details where others can hear breaks patient confidentiality and trust. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T1#GNS124_U6_T1_h8)
